title: Auditing who can still get in
body_md:
## Take stock of what still works

On a Saturday morning you open the security page of your email. The list of signed-in devices is longer than you expected: a phone you traded in, a tablet at your parents’ place, an entry called “Mail client” that you cannot place. That is what an audit is for. It reviews the access that exists today. It is not an annual ritual of changing every password.

Begin with the accounts that give a way into others or could do real damage: your primary email, your password manager, financial services and your work identity. Let impact and evidence set the order. A reported compromise or a reused password calls for quick action. A unique password with nothing wrong with it does not need replacing just because the year turned over.

### A small inventory you will actually use

For each priority account, note the service, the sign-in address you have verified yourself, whether the password is unique, which MFA methods it accepts, where recovery leads, and which devices and sessions are still signed in. Leave the passwords and recovery codes themselves out of the inventory; they belong in the manager and its protected backup. Your password manager’s health view may flag reused or known-compromised entries, so weigh each flag against the real service before you act on it. Have I Been Pwned (HIBP) can list the indexed incidents tied to an email address. It cannot say which password went with that address, and a clean result is not an all-clear.

### What is signed in right now

Next, look at live access. Through the real account settings, remove sessions you do not know and trusted devices you no longer use, but read the device name twice before you call anything an intrusion: one laptop can leave several sessions, and the labels shift over time. Where the service offers them, check app passwords, connected apps and API tokens too. They behave like festival wristbands: once handed out, they keep working until someone cuts them off, and a password change may not revoke every token or session. Before you revoke a grant, find out what uses it, because a legitimate mail client or an automation may stop working. If an unfamiliar session looks like a real intrusion, secure your device, change the credentials involved, check recovery details and forwarding rules, and report it through the provider or your workplace’s channel.

### Keep it easy to repeat

Review the top accounts now and widen the circle later. Run the audit again after a breach, a lost device, a new job or a change of recovery contact, and set a personal reminder for a periodic look instead of counting on a universal “one-hour annual fix.” Plan separately for emergency access to your vault, based on what your password manager offers and what you want. Giving someone emergency access is a deliberate act of trust. It is not a default checkbox, and it is no reason to hand anyone the passphrase that opens your vault.

Close with a short note: which reuse you removed, which MFA or recovery route improved, which suspicious activity needs follow-up, and where a service limits you to weaker controls. The next audit goes faster, and what you do not know stays in plain sight.

widget_config.goal: Put an access audit in order of priority, and tell real signs of compromise from ordinary account activity.
widget_config.today_action: Draft an inventory of five accounts, secrets left out: whether the password is unique, MFA, recovery, sessions and connected apps. Then fix the finding with the biggest impact through the service’s own settings.
widget_config.scope: A general method for learning; service controls, workplace policy and incident response differ. The cases are invented. HIBP coverage is incomplete. Checked 2026-10-20.

sources.title: Have I Been Pwned: Frequently Asked Questions
sources.scope: The service’s own documentation. A listed address does not prove its password leaked, and coverage is incomplete.

sources.scope: US consumer guidance; controls differ by provider.

blocks.title: An unfamiliar token in a developer account
blocks.situation: On the security page of your code-hosting account you find an API token with a name you do not recognise and broad access. The sign-in password is unique, which feels reassuring.
blocks.analysis: A unique password does not neutralise a token that has already been granted. Find out what the token is used for. If it is not yours, revoke it, look through the account’s activity and rotate any secrets it could have reached. Report it to the provider, or to your employer if the account is for work.

blocks.title: Two sessions, one familiar laptop
blocks.situation: Your email service lists two sessions with slightly different browser labels, both from your home area. Both timestamps match times you were really using the laptop.
blocks.analysis: Two rows are not proof of a break-in. Confirm the details in the service’s own device view and sign out any session you cannot explain, but do not call an ordinary duplicate an attack without evidence.

blocks.title: Five accounts, one order of work
blocks.setup: An invented audit sheet. Your email reuses a password; a shop has sent a breach notice; a code-hosting account shows an unknown token; a travel app lists two familiar sessions; your vault has MFA switched on.

choices.text: Give the primary email a unique password in place of the reused one, and review its MFA.
choices.consequence: The reuse with the widest reach is closed.
choices.explanation: The email account may be able to reset several others.

choices.text: Sign out of the two familiar travel-app sessions; it is quick and tidies the sheet.
choices.consequence: The main exposure is still there.
choices.explanation: Familiar sessions are the least urgent line on the sheet. A reused email password comes first.

steps.prompt: Your address turns up in HIBP under the shop’s breach, and the shop’s notice says names and email addresses were exposed, but no passwords. What do you record?

choices.text: Record that the password at the shop has definitely leaked.
choices.consequence: A false conclusion goes into the audit.
choices.explanation: The notice says passwords were not taken, and a listed address alone cannot show otherwise.

choices.text: Record the data categories, check them against the shop’s notice, and do not infer stolen passwords from the email hit.
choices.consequence: The sheet keeps what is known apart from what is not.
choices.explanation: A HIBP address search does not say which password belonged to an account.

steps.prompt: The unknown token on the code-hosting account has broad access. What is the next move?

choices.text: Change the password and assume every token disappears.
choices.explanation: On many services, revoking a token is a separate control.

choices.text: Find out who owns it and when it was last used; revoke it if unowned and check the activity log.
choices.consequence: A possibly live second way in gets dealt with.
choices.explanation: Tokens can work independently of the login password. Check ownership first, so you do not break a known integration blindly.

steps.prompt: Both travel-app sessions match your laptop use. How do you close the review?

choices.text: Check the session details, note the explanation, and sign out only whatever is still unexplained.
choices.consequence: Ordinary activity is not logged as an incident.
choices.explanation: An audit keeps evidence and suspicion apart.

choices.text: Report a confirmed intrusion, since the two session labels look odd.
choices.consequence: The report claims more than the evidence supports.
choices.explanation: One device can hold several sessions.

blocks.debrief: A good audit starts with impact, follows the evidence and looks for the other ways in that still work. Go back to any decision where a warning sign was taken for proof, and try again.

blocks.title: Audit a different set of accounts

questions.prompt: A password is unique and shows no sign of a breach. Is there a reason to change it today?

choices.text: Yes: every password should be changed once a year, whatever the evidence.
choices.explanation: Rotating on a schedule adds work without closing any access that is actually open.

choices.text: Not from the calendar alone. Spend the effort first on signs of compromise, reuse and weak passwords.
choices.explanation: Changing passwords by the calendar is not what an audit is for.

questions.prompt: You change an account password, yet a connected app still has access. Why?

choices.text: App grants and tokens can be independent, and may have to be revoked separately.
choices.explanation: Look in the service’s connected-app settings.

choices.text: A password change always cuts off every connected app.
choices.explanation: Services differ here, so do not assume it.

questions.prompt: A breach database has no entry for your address. What can the audit say?

choices.text: The address, and every account tied to it, is confirmed safe.
choices.explanation: No single database can prove that.

choices.text: No indexed result turned up there, which does not certify that nothing was exposed.
choices.explanation: A database covers only the data it has indexed.
